subject: english
title: Present Perfect
description: Past actions with a present result, experience, and the time markers that decide the tense.

content.title: When to use it
content.body: Use Present Perfect when an action happened in the past but is connected to the present — a result, an experience, or something still going on.

content.title: Form
content.body: have / has + past participle. "I have lived here since 2020." "She has just finished work."

content.title: Watch out
content.body: Present Perfect never takes a finished time marker such as yesterday or in 2019. Those belong to Past Simple.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.explanation: since 2020 marks an action that started in the past and continues now, so Present Perfect is required.

exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?

answers.text: She finished work since an hour.
She is finished work just now.

exercises.explanation: just belongs with Present Perfect. yesterday is a finished time, so it takes Past Simple.

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Have you ever been to Japan?
exercises.explanation: ever + Present Perfect asks about experience at any point in life.

exercises.question: Present Perfect can be used with "yesterday".
exercises.explanation: yesterday is a finished past time, which requires Past Simple: I saw her yesterday.

exercises.question: Complete the question.
exercises.explanation: yet goes with Present Perfect questions, formed with have / has + past participle.

exercises.question: What is the difference between since and for?

answers.text: for is only used in questions
since is for the future, for is for the past
since introduces a starting point, for introduces a duration

exercises.explanation: since 2020, since Monday, since I moved — a point in time. for two years, for ten minutes — a length of time.

exercises.question: Which sentence means she is still away?
exercises.explanation: has gone means she left and has not come back. has been means she visited at some point and has since returned.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.back: Present Perfect takes the third form: I have written
exercises.explanation: The past participle, not the past simple. "I have wrote" is the single most common mistake in this tense.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: I can't get in — I ___ my keys.
exercises.explanation: The past action matters because of its present result — the keys are still missing — so Present Perfect fits.

exercises.question: Which sentence emphasises how long the activity has been going on?

answers.text: I have been debugging this since morning.
I have debugged this since morning.
I am debugging this since morning.

exercises.explanation: The continuous form stresses duration and the activity itself; the simple form stresses the completed result.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: We have ___ deployed the fix, so you can test it.
exercises.explanation: already goes with affirmative statements, yet with questions and negatives: we haven't deployed it yet.

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.

answers.text: I have never worked with Cypress.
I am never working with Cypress.
I did never work with Cypress.

exercises.explanation: Life experience up to now takes Present Perfect, and never carries the negative on its own.

exercises.question: In American English, Past Simple is often used where British English prefers Present Perfect, as in "Did you eat yet?"
exercises.explanation: Both are accepted in practice. In written business English the Present Perfect form is the safer default with just, already and yet.

exercises.question: Why does "I have had three meetings today" use Present Perfect?

answers.text: Today is not over, so the time period still includes the present
Because there is a number in the sentence

exercises.explanation: Unfinished periods — today, this week, this year — take Present Perfect. Once the day is over it becomes "I had three meetings yesterday".

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.back: Present Perfect always takes the third form: I have gone
exercises.explanation: Compare been: I have been to Berlin (and came back) versus I have gone to Berlin (still there).
